tagline: Paul's shortest letter: a personal appeal to a Christian slave owner to receive his returning slave, Onesimus, as a beloved brother.
overview:
Philemon is a single page of papyrus, the shortest of Paul's surviving letters and the most personal. Paul writes from prison to Philemon, a believer who hosts a church in his house, about Onesimus, a slave who belonged to Philemon and who has come to faith through Paul while Paul was in chains. Paul is sending Onesimus back. The whole letter is an appeal for how Philemon should receive him: not merely as returning property, but "as a beloved brother" (verse 16), and even as he would receive Paul himself.

The letter is short, but it is carefully argued. Paul could command, and says so, but chooses to appeal. He offers to pay any debt Onesimus owes, reminds Philemon of his own debt to Paul, writes in front of the whole house church, and ends by asking for a guest room, since he hopes to visit. Every move puts gentle and public pressure on Philemon to act out of love rather than compulsion.

The letter matters for two reasons. It shows the gospel reaching into the most ordinary and most unequal relationship in the Roman household, the bond between master and slave, and refusing to leave it unchanged. And it has a long and painful history of use: it was cited in the nineteenth century both to defend the return of fugitive slaves and to argue that the gospel undermines slavery itself. Reading it honestly means facing both what Paul said and what he did not say.
author: The letter names Paul as its author, with Timothy joining in the greeting, and Paul signs part of it with his own hand (verse 19). Its authenticity is about as secure as anything in the study of the New Testament. Even scholars who doubt that Paul wrote Colossians, Ephesians, or the Pastoral Letters count Philemon among the seven undisputed letters. It was included in Marcion's list of Paul's letters in the second century and in the Muratorian list of accepted writings, usually dated to the late second century. Its brevity and personal subject led a few in the fourth century to question whether it belonged in Scripture at all, and writers such as Jerome and John Chrysostom defended its place, arguing that small letters can carry large truths.
date: Paul writes as a prisoner (verses 1, 9, 10, 13), but the letter does not say where. The traditional view places it during his house arrest in Rome, around AD 60 to 62, which would make it contemporary with Colossians and perhaps Ephesians and Philippians. Many scholars prefer an imprisonment in Ephesus in the mid-50s, pointing out that Ephesus is about a hundred miles from Colossae, which makes a runaway's arrival there and Paul's hope of a quick visit (verse 22) easier to picture. Acts does not record an Ephesian imprisonment, but Paul speaks of many imprisonments (2 Corinthians 11:23). A smaller group suggests Caesarea, around AD 57 to 59. The meaning of the letter does not depend on settling the question.
setting:
Philemon lived in or near Colossae, a town in the Lycus valley of the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey today), near Laodicea and Hierapolis. The link comes from Colossians, which names Onesimus as "one of you" and sends a charge to Archippus, both people who appear in this letter (Colossians 4:9, 17). Philemon was wealthy enough to own at least one slave and to host a congregation in his house, the normal meeting place for churches before there were church buildings.

Slavery in the Roman world was pervasive and was not based on race. People became slaves through capture in war, piracy, debt, being born to an enslaved mother, or being abandoned as infants. Estimates of how much of the population was enslaved vary widely. Slaves worked as field hands and miners but also as household servants, teachers, doctors, and business managers, and freeing slaves (manumission) was common, especially in cities. None of this made the institution gentle. A slave was legally property, could be beaten, sold, or separated from family, and had no right to marry in law. A runaway could be hunted, branded, or worse. Roman legal writers, whose opinions were later gathered in Justinian's Digest, distinguished a fugitive from a slave who left to seek out a friend of the master to plead on his behalf, and some scholars think that distinction may describe Onesimus.
purpose: Paul writes to secure a welcome for Onesimus and a reconciliation between him and Philemon on a new footing. What exactly Paul hoped for is debated. At the least he asks that Philemon receive Onesimus as a brother and not punish him. Verse 13 and the remark that Philemon will do "even more than I ask" (verse 21) suggest to many readers that Paul hoped Onesimus would be freed or sent back to assist him in his work. How Onesimus came to be with Paul is also debated. The traditional view, found in early interpreters such as John Chrysostom, is that he ran away, perhaps after stealing (verse 18). Others think he sought Paul out as a friend of his master to intercede in a dispute, or that Philemon had sent him to Paul. John Knox (1935) argued that the owner was actually Archippus. Allen Dwight Callahan has argued that Onesimus was not a slave at all but Philemon's estranged brother, a reading most scholars have not followed.
story: Philemon comes after the Pastoral Letters in the order of the English Bible, which arranges Paul's letters to churches first and then his letters to individuals, roughly by length. In the story of the early church it belongs with Colossians: the same messengers, Tychicus and Onesimus, probably carried both letters to the Lycus valley. It shows in miniature what Galatians 3:28 and Colossians 3:11 state in principle, that in Christ the categories of slave and free no longer define who a person is before God or in the church. Its questions about how the gospel works on social institutions carry forward through the whole history of the church.
christ: The letter never explains the gospel in the abstract; it acts it out. Paul places himself between the offended master and the guilty or vulnerable slave and says, "charge it to my account" (verse 18). Readers from Martin Luther onward have seen in that sentence a picture of what Christ does for sinners, taking their debt on himself and presenting them to the Father as he would present himself. That is an analogy, not an allegory Paul intended, but it rests on the pattern of his theology. More directly, the phrase "in Christ" and "in the Lord" runs through the letter: it is union with Christ that makes Onesimus Paul's child, Philemon's brother, and a partner in the church.
reading: Read Philemon aloud in one sitting and listen to its tact. It is a real letter to real people, and its persuasion works through courtesy, wordplay, friendship, and public accountability rather than direct command. Watch for the pun on Onesimus's name (which means useful) in verse 11, and for the language of debt, partnership, and refreshed hearts. Two misreadings should be avoided. One treats the letter as an endorsement of slavery because Paul sends Onesimus back and does not denounce the institution. The other reads it as a direct command to emancipate, which Paul never quite states. The letter is better read as the gospel planting within a household a relationship that the institution of slavery could not contain.

structure.title: Greeting
structure.summary: Paul the prisoner and Timothy greet Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church in Philemon's house.

structure.title: Thanksgiving for Philemon's love
structure.summary: Paul thanks God for Philemon's faith and for the love that has refreshed the hearts of the saints, preparing the ground for his request.

structure.title: The appeal for Onesimus
structure.summary: Paul appeals rather than commands, sends Onesimus back as his own heart, asks Philemon to receive him as a beloved brother, and offers to pay whatever he owes.

structure.title: Greetings and blessing
structure.summary: Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke send greetings, and Paul closes with a blessing of grace.

themes.title: A new relationship in Christ
themes.body: The heart of the letter is verse 16: Onesimus returns "no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother." The social arrangement has not yet changed, but the relationship inside it has been redefined. Philemon and Onesimus now share one Lord, one table, and one family, and Paul asks Philemon to let that new reality govern how he treats the man who belongs to him in law.

themes.title: Persuasion through love
themes.body: Paul says he could order Philemon to do the right thing but prefers to appeal "on the basis of love" (verse 9). He wants Philemon's goodness to be freely given, not forced (verse 14). The letter models a kind of authority that refuses to coerce and instead calls on a friend's own faith, while still being frank about what is expected.

themes.title: Substitution and debt
themes.body: Paul steps in to cover whatever Onesimus owes and writes the pledge in his own hand. The language of accounts, debts, and repayment turns a legal matter into an act of costly friendship. Christians have long heard in it an echo of the substitution at the heart of the gospel.

themes.title: The gospel and social institutions
themes.body: Philemon raises a question the church has argued about ever since: does the gospel only change hearts within existing structures, or does it undermine unjust structures themselves? The letter was quoted on both sides of the American debate over slavery. Most readers today see in it a seed whose logic, a slave who is a brother "in the Lord" and "in person", could not in the end coexist with ownership of one person by another.

keyChapters.why: The whole letter is one chapter: Paul's appeal for Onesimus, a slave who has become a brother, and his offer to take on Onesimus's debt himself.
